name: Dimethicone
lead: Dimethicone, also known as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or dimethylpolysiloxane, is a silicone polymer and a type of silicone oil. It ranges from a pourable liquid to a rubbery semi-solid depending on chain length, and it is hydrophobic and optically clear.[1] On skin it leaves a thin, smooth, water-repellent film, which is why it is found in moisturizers, primers and barrier creams, and on hair it coats the strand to add slip and shine.[1][9]

In skin and hair products it is widely used as a skin-protectant and conditioning ingredient, listed in moisturizing lotions and sometimes present at concentrations up to about 15 percent, and in shampoos and conditioners to add slip and shine.[1] The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel has concluded that dimethicone and related polymers are safe as used in cosmetic formulations.[1]

Published human studies of dimethicone concern medical uses such as incontinence-associated dermatitis and head lice rather than appearance outcomes. Consumers mainly encounter it as an ingredient in moisturizers and hair products, and product labels list it as a skin protectant.[2]

paras: Dimethicone has the formula CH3[Si(CH3)2O]nSi(CH3)3, with chains capped by trimethylsilyl groups. Commercial material is made by base-catalysed ring-opening polymerisation of cyclic siloxanes. Viscosity rises with chain length, from a thin oil to a rubbery semi-solid.[1]
It is hydrophobic and is not appreciably swollen by water or alcohols, although many organic solvents swell it.[1]

Dimethicone is common in moisturizing lotions, often listed for skin protection, and is described as feeling lighter than typical plant or mineral oils.[1] In hair care it adds shine and slipperiness to shampoos and conditioners; an amino-modified relative, amodimethicone, is described as a more effective conditioner for damaged hair.[1] Dimethicone/methicone copolymer is also used as a coating on nano-sized titanium dioxide particles in sunscreens.[4]

Because it is a protectant film-former, it also appears in barrier products. A systematic review of contact dermatitis prevention found that barrier creams containing dimethicone or perfluoropolyethers prevent irritant contact dermatitis,[10] and a review of barrier-repair creams lists dimethicone alongside ceramides, hyaluronic acid and petrolatum among the substances used to support a damaged skin barrier.[11]

Activated dimethicone (simethicone) is used as an antifoaming agent in over-the-counter medicines and in food, and dimethicone is used as a head-lice treatment, thought to act by blocking water excretion rather than by suffocation.[1] It also appears in condom lubricants, sealants and silicone greases.[1]

Irritant dermatitis and skin protection. A 2005 systematic review of 49 studies concluded that barrier creams containing dimethicone or perfluoropolyethers prevent irritant contact dermatitis, noting that well-controlled outcome-blinded studies were still needed.[10] A randomised cross-over study of 73 military health care workers compared a hydrocolloid dressing with dimethicone cream as facial skin protectants under N95 masks; participants wearing a mask alone reported more adverse skin reactions than with either protectant, and mask fit test failure rates did not differ.[12]

Incontinence-associated dermatitis. A randomised trial in 11 nursing-home wards in Belgium (141 residents analysed, 120 days) compared a washcloth impregnated with 3 percent dimethicone against water and pH-neutral soap, using a 10-point severity tool for area, redness and erosion depth.[5]

Eczema. A 2016 pilot study of 25 adults with mild-to-moderate eczema used a moisturizer containing dimethicone, shea butter, glycerin, sodium PCA, hyaluronate, ceramides and botanical anti-inflammatories three times daily for two weeks and reported significant improvement in signs and symptoms; because the product is a multi-ingredient formulation the result cannot be attributed to dimethicone alone.[13]

Head lice and medicine. Dimethicone-based lotions are used against head lice, and registered trials compared a 4 percent dimethicone foam with permethrin cream rinse (31 participants).[6] Simethicone, an activated form, has been trialled for gastric foam reduction before endoscopy and for reflux oesophagitis alongside antacids.[7][14] No published trial found examines dimethicone for improving facial appearance, skin texture or hair quality in healthy people. A minipig study of sunscreens found no significant dermal penetration of titanium dioxide, including particles coated with dimethicone/methicone copolymer.[4]

The term silicone was coined in 1901 by the chemist F. S. Kipping, who named a polydiphenylsiloxane by analogy with the ketone benzophenone; siloxane is now the preferred chemical term [15]. James Franklin Hyde is called the father of silicones for launching the silicone industry in the 1930s, and his work led to Dow Corning, a joint venture of Dow Chemical and Corning Glass Works [15].

Dimethicone became one of the best-known silicone polymers, with uses ranging from lubricants and sealants to breast implant shells (a PDMS elastomer filled with silicone gel or saline), antifoam agents in food as E900, and condom lubricants [1]. In personal care, silicones are widely used in skincare and colour cosmetics, shaving products and hair care; amino-modified relatives such as amodimethicone act as conditioners that soften hair and reduce frizz, while phenyl-modified silicones add shine [15].

Dimethicone's cosmetic popularity rests on its light feel compared with plant and mineral oils and on its use in primers, moisturizers and hair conditioners [1][16]. Dermatologists quoted in a Healthline explainer describe it as filling in the look of fine lines, helping makeup go on evenly with a matte finish, and coating hair strands to smooth the cuticle for shine and some heat protection [16]. Product labels in drugstore skin care list it as a skin-protectant active, as on a baby oatmeal lotion label [2].

Some consumers worry that a film-forming ingredient could trap oil and dirt and contribute to breakouts. The same explainer describes dimethicone as non-comedogenic, quotes the dermatologist Peterson Pierre saying he knows of no data to substantiate public concern and considers it safe, and notes that its large molecular weight makes skin absorption very unlikely [16]. It also reports that dimethicone can build up on hair and that dermatologist Jessie Cheung suggests an occasional clarifying shampoo [16].

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel concluded that dimethicone and related polymers are safe as used in cosmetic formulations, and the European Food Safety Authority's 2020 re-evaluation of E 900 found no safety concerns for reported food uses while recommending a limit on residual cyclic siloxanes from manufacturing.[1]
Silicone granuloma of facial tissues has been described in case reports following injection of liquid silicone, which is a different route and use from topical dimethicone.[8]

Referencing an industrial chemistry encyclopedia, Wikipedia notes that no marked harmful effects on organisms have been recorded for siloxanes; PDMS is not biodegradable but is captured in wastewater treatment.[1]

timeline.event: F. S. Kipping coins the term silicone [15].
James Franklin Hyde launches the silicone industry; Dow Corning later forms from Dow Chemical and Corning Glass Works [15].
Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel finds most OTC products contain under 15 percent dimethicone and concludes it is safe in cosmetics [16].
EFSA re-evaluation of E 900 finds no safety concern for reported food uses [1].

lore.intro: Dimethicone comes up in skincare and haircare discussion as a primer, filler and shine ingredient, and as a frequently debated one for people prone to breakouts [16].

claims.claim: Dimethicone fills in fine lines and gives a smooth base under makeup
claims.believers: Users and cosmetic marketing describe primers and moisturizers with dimethicone as blurring texture and helping foundation go on evenly [16].
claims.experts: Dermatologists quoted by Healthline describe a filling and smoothing effect at the skin surface; no published trial has measured dimethicone for facial appearance in healthy people [16].

claims.claim: Silicones clog pores and cause breakouts
claims.believers: Some skincare users say the film traps oil, sweat and dirt and avoid silicones for that reason [16].
claims.experts: A dermatologist quoted by Healthline says there is no data to substantiate the concern; the article describes dimethicone as non-comedogenic [16].

claims.claim: Dimethicone gives hair shine and slip but can build up
claims.believers: Hair-care users report glossier, easier-to-comb hair, and some report weighed-down hair after repeated use [16].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes silicone conditioners as improving softness and reducing frizz, and a dermatologist suggests occasional clarifying shampoo for buildup [15][16].

card.summary: A silicone oil used as a skin protectant and hair-smoothing ingredient; trials cover medical uses, not appearance outcomes.
card.note: Cosmetic safety panels rate it safe as used; liquid silicone injection is a separate, documented source of granulomas.

quick.overview:
Dimethicone is a silicone oil found in many moisturizers, primers, shampoos and conditioners. It gives a smooth, slippery feel and forms a water-repellent film on skin and hair.

Published human trials involve medical uses such as dermatitis and head lice; none were found testing it for improving appearance in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: It is a long-chain silicone polymer that is hydrophobic and leaves a thin protective layer on the surface of skin or hair, which accounts for its conditioning and smoothing effect.
quick.risks: The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded it is safe as used in cosmetics. Silicone granulomas reported in the literature arise from injected liquid silicone, not topical use. It is not biodegradable but is removed in wastewater treatment.

chain: Spreads as a thin hydrophobic silicone film
Skin feels smoother and holds in water; hair strands gain slip and shine
Smoother-looking skin surface and glossier hair
angle.text: Dimethicone is used for the immediate look and feel it gives: a smooth, silky skin surface under makeup or moisturizer, and shinier, easier-to-comb hair. It works at the surface rather than changing skin biology.
